Top Takeaways for Clinicians from the
KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline
10 for Blood Pressure Management in CKD*
Standardized office BP measurement
Standardized BP measurement emphasizes the importance of appropriate prepara-
between routine office BP and standardized office BP is highly variable; therefore, it
1 tions and the measurement technique, not the type of device. The relationship
is not possible to apply a correction factor to translate a given routine BP value to a
standardized BP value.
Home BP monitoring
HBPM may be particularly important for the management of BP when a
clinic visit is not practical, for example, during the coronavirus disease 2019
(COVID-19) pandemic. However, at present, HBPM should only be used to • No smoking, caffeine, or exercise for ≥30 min
2 • Quiet room (no talking by patient or observer)
complement standardized office measurement and not guide treatment before measurement
• Empty bladder
decisions, if standardized office BP is available. • Relax for >5 min
BP target in CKD not treated with dialysis
Adults with high BP and CKD should be treated to a target SBP <120 mm Hg No talking during rest period
techniques. When measured under standardized conditions, targeting SBP Cuff to fit arm size (small, usual, large)
3 which must be measured using standardized office BP preparations and and between measurements
Arm bare and resting.
<120 mm Hg reduces the risks of CV events and all-cause mortality in CKD; Mid-arm at midpoint of the sternum
however, the effects on progression of kidney disease are uncertain.

The SBP target of <120 mm Hg also applies to the subgroups of older Validated oscillometric
or manual auscultatory
adults and those with increased albuminuria. The balance of benefits device2,3, calibrated
and harms is less certain in people with CKD G5 and in those with severe- periodically
4 ly increased albuminuria (A3). Feet flat on floor
BP target in patients with diabetes
The benefits of intensive BP lowering are less certain among patients
5 with concomitant CKD and diabetes, compared to patients with CKD Lifestyle
without diabetes. • Salt intake <2 g/d (<90 mmol/d)
• Physical activity: 150 min/week moderate-intensity
Antihypertensive agents in CKD
Pediatric patients
RASi (ACEi or ARB) should be used in patients with CKD and increased
≤50th percentile for ACEi or ARB
6 albuminuria, with or without diabetes. The evidence for use of RASi in 24 h MAP by ABPM
patients with moderately increased albuminuria is lower in quality than
age, sex, and height
in severely increased albuminuria.
Adults with CKD with and without diabetes
Lifestyle interventions ACEi or ARB
7 Low sodium intake (<2 g/day) and moderate-intensity physical activity SBP <120 mm Hg • G1–G4, A3 without
(≥150 min/week) are suggested in accordance with recommendations for diabetes (1B)
the general population. • G1–G4, A2 without
diabetes (2C)
• G1–G4, A2 or A3
with diabetes (1B)
BP target in KTR
For adult kidney transplant recipients, a target of <130/<80 mm Hg, using
8 standardized office measurement, is still a reasonable goal. A lower SBP Adult kidney transplant recipients
goal (<120 mm Hg) for kidney transplant recipients would require
Dihydropyridine
additional data on the risks and benefits in this population. <130/<80 mm Hg
CCB or ARB
Targets Preferred drugs
Antihypertensive agents in KTR
9 Dihydropyridine CCB or ARB should be used as the first-line antihyper-
tensive agent in adult kidney transplant recipients given their efficacy in
and the importance of preventing graft loss.
BP management in children
BP target in children with high BP and CKD should be lowered to ≤50th
10 percentile for age, sex, and height according to 24-hour MAP by ABPM.
When ABPM is not available, standardized auscultatory office measure-
ment should be used to target SBP <90th percentile.
*The KDIGO Guideline for the Management of BP is applicable to patients with CKD not receiving dialysis. ABPM, ambulatory blood pressure monitoring;
